edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7    1 (on every page; page number right-aligned)
edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / <id>' on every page instead of the bare right-aligned page number.

edits.quote: It is your turn with a bigger pile.
edits.fix: Delete 'with a bigger pile'; the pictures of 10, 11 and 12 counters already show it. Keep 'It is your turn.' and the task sentence.

edits.quote: Show every different way a game with 4 counters can go, and then every way a game with 5 counters can go. Taking 1 then 2 is different from taking 2 then 1.
edits.fix: As written this is a counting exercise (5 ways for 4, 8 ways for 5) that never asks who wins, so it breaks the trap sequence between P5 and P7. Add one sentence tying it to winning, e.g. 'Put a star by every way where the first player wins,' or recast it as 'You go first with 4. Show every way the game can go if you play to win, whatever your partner does.'

edits.quote: Now there are two piles, and on your turn you take 1 or 2 counters from one pile.
edits.fix: Add 'Whoever takes the very last counter on the table wins.' A child who thinks emptying one pile ends the game gets the wrong answer for the 1 and 1, 1 and 2, and 1 and 4 pairs.

edits.quote: Diagram: in each pair box '1st' is printed directly under the left pile and '2nd' directly under the right pile.
edits.fix: Center one '1st   2nd' choice below the whole pair box, as in P2. As drawn the words look like names for the two piles ('first pile', 'second pile') rather than the two players.

k-1.summary: A strong K–1 band with real work: traps for {1, 2} from 1 to 20, a test of a fixed move, a rule change to {1, 2, 3}, two-pile positions including the surprising 1-and-4 loss, the copycat strategy for 6 and 6, and the misère version. All answers check out. Edits are light: P6 drifts into counting game sequences without asking who wins, and the two-pile page needs the last-counter rule stated and the 1st/2nd labels moved off the individual piles.

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7    1 (on every page; page number right-aligned)
edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / <id>' on every page.

edits.quote: Now there are two piles. On each turn, a player takes 1 or 2 counters from one of the piles.
edits.fix: Add 'The game goes on until both piles are empty; whoever takes the very last counter wins.' Otherwise the 4-and-1 pair, which is a second-player win, can be misread as a first-player win by emptying the 1-pile.

edits.quote: Diagram: in each pair box 'First' is printed under the left pile and 'Second' under the right pile.
edits.fix: Center one 'First   Second' choice below each pair box so the words cannot be read as labels for the piles.

edits.quote: When the two piles are the same size, which player can always win? Explain why. (pairs shown: 4 and 4, 4 and 2, 4 and 1, 5 and 3)
edits.fix: Only one equal pair is shown for a general claim. Add two or three more pairs, e.g. 3 and 3, 5 and 5, 5 and 2, 6 and 3. The page has room, and the extra contrasting examples make this a full five-minute problem.

edits.quote: Now whoever takes the last counter loses.
edits.fix: The shared rule 'If you cannot take any counters, you lose' would make the player facing the empty pile lose, which contradicts this. Add 'The game ends when the last counter is taken.'

grades-2-3.summary: This band is right on the outline: it checks Lee's and Mo's claims against every reply, tests Jo's and Kai's {1, 3, 4} moves with full game trees, classifies 1 to 20, extends to 30, 50, 61 and 100 through the period-7 pattern, and covers the parity game {1, 3, 5}, two piles, the open 'find a rule for multiples of 5' problem and the misère version. All answers are correct. Edits are minor and all on the two-pile page and the misère rule.

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7    1 (on every page; page number right-aligned)
edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / <id>' on every page.

edits.quote: Change the rule so that whoever takes the last counter loses.
edits.fix: Add 'The game ends when the last counter is taken,' so it does not clash with the shared rule 'If you cannot take any counters, you lose.'

grades-4-5.summary: This is an excellent upper band. It classifies {1, 3, 4} to 24 and extends to 100, 1000 and 2026, compares four rules (including {1, 2, 4} matching {1, 2}), disproves the greedy plan in three games and proves it in {1, 3, 5}, explains why the pattern repeats forever, has a complete inverse problem (answers {1,2,3} with any subset of {5,6}), compares misère versions, and fills two-pile grids whose {1, 3, 4} pairs (1-3, 1-8, 3-8, 2-7, 4-6) bring in Grundy values without naming them. Every answer checks out, and only the footer and one misère sentence need touching.

overall.strongest: The grades 4–5 band develops periodicity, rule changes, greedy failure, an inverse classification and two-pile sums through a correct, well-sequenced set of open problems with plain wording.
overall.weakest: The two-pile pages in K–1 and grades 2–3 leave unstated that play continues until the very last counter on the table, and they print First/Second under the individual piles, where they read as pile labels; the K–1 sequence-counting problem (P6) also drifts from the trap idea.
